headline: High: OpenBBTerminal’s MCP/API surfaces can create data-leakage and cascading-error risk when paired with a non-writing data-engineering course agent, while prompt-injection and direct capability conflict are limited.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a course repo with no I/O surfaces or runtime, while agent B exposes MCP/REST/stdin-stdout and can consume external content. There is no documented shared channel between them, so only an unusual manual bridge or copied content could inject instructions into B. The pathway is plausible but narrow.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies A-generated text into B's MCP/CLI input, injection becomes possible.
IF a shared filesystem or message queue is added between the agents, the risk increases.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Do not paste A outputs directly into B prompts.
Disable MCP routes that accept untrusted text where possible.
Add a short provenance note before any copied content.
requires-engineering: add content provenance tagging between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B touches financial, licensed, and public data and can call APIs/MCP servers; agent A is a data-engineering course repo with no data classes listed. There is no shared filesystem documented, but B’s networked surfaces mean any copied A content or shared workspace could leak sensitive B context to external services. The interaction is inferred, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF A and B are placed in the same shared workspace, leakage risk increases.
IF B is configured to send prompts or file contents to external APIs, sensitive context can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Keep B’s sensitive datasets out of shared folders.
Review MCP/API destinations before enabling them.
Run B with the smallest possible context window.
Separate credentials and API keys per agent.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator level.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A has no write, shell, or network capabilities; agent B cannot write the filesystem, modify git state, or spawn subprocesses. With no overlapping mutable write surface, direct capability conflict is largely blocked. The only remaining conflict is operational, not technical, so low is sufficient.
conditions: IF an orchestrator grants both agents write access to the same external resource, conflict risk rises.
IF B is wrapped by a separate tool that adds write privileges, the assessment changes.
mitigations: Keep both agents read-only where possible.
Avoid shared mutable directories.
Do not grant git write access to B.
Run one instance at a time for shared resources.
requires-engineering: add locking for any future shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B can act through MCP/REST APIs and may treat upstream text as operational input, while agent A can supply course material or generated explanations. There is no verification layer documented between them, so A’s output could be forwarded into B’s workflows and acted on without checking. The blast radius is multiple work products, not just one file.
conditions: IF A’s text is used as an input source for B’s analysis or automation, cascading errors become likely.
IF B is configured to execute actions from MCP/API responses without review, the risk increases.
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A outputs.
Label A content as untrusted input in prompts.
Use a validation checklist for any B action derived from A.
Limit B to read-only analysis modes.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B explicitly touches financial and licensed data and exposes API/MCP surfaces; agent A is an open-source course repo with no compliance controls or data classes listed. Because B’s residency, retention, and licensing obligations are not documented here, pairing them can create policy mismatch if A-derived content is mixed into B workflows. The other agent is cited only to show the source of the mismatch.
conditions: IF regulated or licensed B data is processed alongside A-derived materials, policy mismatch becomes relevant.
IF B is deployed under a residency or retention policy not reflected in A, compliance gaps widen.
mitigations: Separate regulated B data from A materials.
Check retention settings before sharing outputs.
Document which data classes each agent may touch.
Avoid mixing licensed data with course content.
requires-engineering: map residency and retention controls per workflow.
